name: Guiziga Muturwa
overview: Having come from Sudan via Gudur and Mokong, the Guiziga of Muturwa live among the Gudur and the Guidar, in a landscape of sacred mountains such as the “Finger of God”. Patrilineal, formerly organised under the authority of the lulo into classes of blacksmiths and cultivators, they honour their ancestors through the mulvring and celebrate the great festivals of Diguila and Muvulgum.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: The group lives with the Gudur and the Guidar; despite variations, the Guiziga speech varieties remain mutually intelligible.
Guiziga is found in the Diamaré and the Mayo-Tsanaga, and as far as Nigeria.
Traditionally, people marry among the Guiziga but from different clans; today, with everybody.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The “Finger of God” mountain is the group's great religious symbol, even though Islamisation has gradually erased it.
Having come from Sudan, the Guiziga arrived at Gudur via Mokong, then spread across the Far North, notably towards Maroua; they keep ties with relatives who stayed along the route.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Before Islam, the group was hierarchical under the authority of the lulo, with classes of blacksmiths and farmers.
The king only makes consensual decisions, after consultation.
Young people, elders and women form groups that communicate through spokespersons.
The Muturwa Gulundjè are in charge of the dead; all women learn the role of mourner from childhood: announcing the death, mourning the deceased, retracing their life.
Formerly, the wife did not eat from the same dish as her husband, and the children had their own corner.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's family; never marriage within the same family.
Formerly, marriages were decided very early by the fathers.
A girl could be reserved from birth by the placing of a piece of wood; the boy's family then helped with the work in the fields, then the boy's father came to ask for her.
Bride price: cockerels and goats for modest families, an ox for the better-off.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Two cults: the mulvring for the ancestors (invoked in February) and the kuli to implore God.
Sacred sites: mountains (Finger of God, Moimotokol), places of refuge, water points, forests.
A birth is a wish: only life will say what it means. Death leads back to the ancestors, who are invoked and fed during festivals and hardships.
Taboos: incest, striking one's parents, killing (outside codified revenge, the tuang).
A distinction is made between great sins (murder, incest) and minor sins (adultery).
The diviner communicates with the mulvring and the kuli.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Activities: hunting, forging, farming, crafts; spinning and dyeing of cotton.
The land falls under the master of the land, the Muturwa Guboy.
Craftsmanship is an ancestral practice.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: From the loincloth to cotton fabrics, then to wrappers.
Traditional medicine is still frequented, but healing comes from God.
Beauty: the sturdy, strong, resilient man; the woman with a high bust who is obedient.
Courtship: cleanliness, talent as a dancer and worker; ornaments of ostrich feathers, beads and jewellery.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: badogou dodong, badang guitiki (twins' festival), gagang (weddings and mutual help in the fields, in the rainy season).
Instruments: wood, drum, snail shells.
Dances: bada guititi, tchaval, broum guititi.
Festivals: Diguila (harvests) and Muvulgum, the largest, with many rites.

sections.title: The names
items: Names specific to twins: Maissai and Loa for boys, Kutvu and Loa for a boy-girl pair.
A rite of “depositing” the child precedes the giving of the name.
One does not change name, but titles are added to it according to the actions accomplished.

lessons.title: Who are the Guiziga Muturwa? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Guiziga Muturwa community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Guiziga Muturwa community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Guiziga Muturwa community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Guiziga Muturwa community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Guiziga Muturwa community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Guiziga Muturwa call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The group lives with the Gudur and the Guidar; despite variations, the Guiziga speech varieties remain mutually intelligible. • Guiziga is found in Diamaré and Mayo-Tsanaga, and as far as Nigeria. • Traditionally, people marry among the Guiziga but from different clans; today, with everyone. • The mountain “Finger of God” is the group's great religious symbol, even though Islamisation has gradually erased it. • Coming from Sudan, the Guiziga arrived at Gudur via Mokong, then spread across the Far North, notably towards Maroua; they keep ties with relatives who stayed along the route.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Having come from Sudan via Gudur and Mokong, the Guiziga of Muturwa live among the Gudur and the Guidar, in a landscape of sacred mountains such as the “Finger of God”. Patrilineal, formerly organised under the authority of the lulo into classes of blacksmiths and cultivators, they honour their ancestors through the mulvring and celebrate the great festivals of Diguila and Muvulgum.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Guiziga Muturwa community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Guiziga Muturwa
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Guiziga Muturwa organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Guiziga Muturwa village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Guiziga Muturwa organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Guiziga Muturwa village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Before Islam, the group was hierarchical under the authority of the lulo, with classes of blacksmiths and farmers. • The king takes only consensual decisions, after consultation. • Young people, elders and women form groups that communicate through spokespersons. • The Muturwa Gulundjè are in charge of the dead; all women learn from childhood the role of mourner: announcing the death, weeping for the deceased, retracing his or her life. • Formerly, the wife did not eat from the same dish as her husband, and the children had their own corner.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Before Islam, the group was hierarchical under the authority of the lulo, with classes of blacksmiths and farmers. The king takes only consensual decisions, after consultation. Young people, elders and women form groups that communicate through spokespersons.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Guiziga Muturwa, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Guiziga Muturwa
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Guiziga Muturwa, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Guiziga Muturwa.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Guiziga Muturwa, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Guiziga Muturwa.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: abaga sauce, ambaka sauce. • Drinks: to be collected from the elders. • Activities: hunting, blacksmithing, farming, crafts; cotton spinning and dyeing.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Guiziga Muturwa mainly eat abaga sauce, ambaka sauce. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Guiziga Muturwa: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Guiziga Muturwa
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Guiziga Muturwa welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Guiziga Muturwa family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Guiziga Muturwa welcome a child, give it a name and mark its entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A child has just been born in a Guiziga Muturwa family. How will they be named, and how will they become an adult?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Names specific to twins: Maissai and Loa for boys, Kutvu and Loa for a boy-girl pair. • A “deposit” rite for the child precedes the giving of the name. • One does not change name, but titles are added according to deeds accomplished. • A birth is a wish: only life will tell what it means. Death brings one back to the ancestors, who are invoked and fed during festivals and trials. • Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's family; never marriage within the same family.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Names specific to twins: Maissai and Loa for boys, Kutvu and Loa for a boy-girl pair. A rite of “depositing” the child precedes the giving of the name. One does not change one's name, but titles are added to it according to the actions accomplished.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

student.memo: Among the Guiziga Muturwa, traditional dances (bada guititi, tchaval, broum guititi) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, wood, snail shells. Festival(s): harvests, Muvulgum.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Guiziga Muturwa
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Guiziga Muturwa, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Guiziga Muturwa. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Guiziga Muturwa, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Guiziga Muturwa. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Activities: hunting, forging, farming, crafts; cotton spinning and dyeing. • The land belongs to the master of the land, the Muturwa Guboy. • Crafts are an ancestral practice.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Activities: hunting, forging, farming, crafts; spinning and dyeing of cotton. The land belongs to the master of the land, the Muturwa Guboy.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Guiziga Muturwa's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Guiziga Muturwa
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Guiziga Muturwa, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Guiziga Muturwa. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Guiziga Muturwa, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Guiziga Muturwa. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Two forms of worship: the mulvring for the ancestors (invoked in February) and the kuli to implore God. • Sacred sites: mountains (Doigt de Dieu, Moimotokol), places of refuge, water points, forests. • A birth is a wish: only life will tell what it means. Death leads back to the ancestors, who are invoked and fed at festivals and in times of hardship. • Taboos: incest, striking one's parents, killing (outside codified vengeance, the tuang). • A distinction is made between great sins (murder, incest) and minor sins (adultery).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Two cults: the mulvring for the ancestors (invoked in February) and the kuli to implore God. Sacred sites: mountains (Finger of God, Moimotokol), places of refuge, water points, forests.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Guiziga Muturwa (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Guiziga
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Guiziga Muturwa and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Guiziga Muturwa family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Guiziga Muturwa greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Guiziga Muturwa family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Guiziga. • Greeting formulae: Mbirke ; djam = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Ki hinam lee = morning greeting (one person); Djam djam koum = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Mbula, Cuw, Makir, Mufad, Zlum. • One does not change one's name, but titles are added to it according to the deeds accomplished.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Guiziga are the first steps towards communicating with the Guiziga Muturwa. The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Guiziga.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Guiziga are the first steps towards communicating with the Guiziga Muturwa. The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
